10StepsinExcelforWoS: Streamlining bibliometric analysis in web of science
using Microsoft excel
Tsair-Wei Chien <sup>a</sup>, Willy Chou <sup>b,c,*</sup>
<sup>a</sup> Department of Medical Research, Chi Mei Medical Center, Tainan, Taiwan
<sup>b</sup> Department of Leisure and Sports Management, CTBC University, Tainan, Taiwan
<sup>c</sup> Department of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation, Liouying Chi-Mei Hospital, Tainan 736, Taiwan
A R T I C L E I N F O
Keywords:
Bibliometric analysis
Web of science
Excel VBA
Data wrangling
Visualization framework
A B S T R A C T
Numerous bibliometric studies utilize professional software to generate visualizations from specialized text files
downloaded from the Web of Science Core Collection (WoSCC). However, when using Microsoft Excel (MS Excel)
files exported from WoSCC, researchers often face a series of manual and cumbersome data preprocessing tasks
that hinder efficiency. To address this challenge, this study proposes a streamlined frame-
work—10StepsinExcelforWoS—to facilitate bibliometric analysis using MS Excel. A total of 1719 articles
published in the journal of SoftwareX between 2017 and 2025 were retrieved from WoSCC. The proposed
method involves 10 sequential steps implemented via Visual Basic for Applications (VBA) within Excel to
wrangle the data. Two types of visualizations were demonstrated: (1) a summary report for performance analysis
and (2) Kano and Sankey diagrams to identify dominant entities in bibliometric research since 2017. Key findings
identified the United States as the leading country; Delft University of Technology (Netherlands) as the top
institution; the Department of Computer Science as the most prevalent affiliation—appearing across 60 uni
versities for first authors and 42 for corresponding authors; Wojciech Salabun (Poland) as the most prolific
author; and “MODEL” as the most prominent keyword.This study concludes that the 10StepsinExcelforWoS
offers a practical, transparent, efficient, and reproducible workflow for conducting nuanced bibliometric ana-
lyses directly in MS Excel.

spans.content: 1. Motivation and significance
In recent years, bibliometric analysis has become a cornerstone in
evaluating academic productivity, research trends, and scholarly impact
across disciplines [1]. While professional tools like CiteSpace[2], VOS-
viewer[3], and Bibliometrix[4] are widely adopted to generate visuali-
zations from standardized text files exported from the Web of Science
Core Collection (WoSCC)[5], their functionality often relies on specific
file formats and predefined workflows. In contrast, Excel-exported
WoSCC files, although widely accessible, typically require laborious
manual preprocessing steps before they can be used for in-depth bib
liometric research(e.g., publications [1,6–8] that rely on the R platform
[9]). These steps include data filtering, field standardization, metadata
restructuring, and summary table generation—tasks that are both
time-consuming and prone to inconsistency, especially for novice users.
1.1. Research gaps in current bibliometric workflows
Despite the maturity of bibliometric software, several gaps remain in
the practical workflow for researchers aiming to use Excel-based
outputs:
(1) Lack of streamlined preprocessing for Excel data: Researchers
often face tedious, repetitive operations when attempting to clean
and structure raw Excel data from WoSCC, which hinders
reproducibility and deters early-career scholars.
(2) Insufficient integration of VBA-based automation: Few
studies leverage Microsoft Excel’s scripting capabilities (i.e., Vi-
sual Basic for Applications, VBA) to automate and simplify these
bibliometric tasks.
(3) Limited reproducible frameworks for non-specialists: Most
bibliometric tools require some level of software familiarity (e.g.,
Java, R, Python), which creates a barrier for users with limited
programming backgrounds. Moreover, the non-transparency of
the data source will hinder the reproducibility of some corre
sponding studies [10].
(4) Ranking only for metadata elements: Traditional bibliometric
methods rely on frequency-based rankings, lacking analytical
depth. The underused dominance coefficient (DC) [11,12] can
quantify gaps between top-ranked elements.
1.2. Addressing the practical needs of bibliometric researchers
Exploring graphs (e.g., slope, summary report, or other charts) is
crucial for researchers, as they offer a clearer view of complex temporal
relationships in bibliometric data [1]. For example, adopting slope
graphs enhances the interpretability of time-series data, improves trend
identification, and conveys comparative dynamics more effectively.
However, methods for extracting core elements are based on sufficient
data collected with datasets (e.g., those in MS Excel).That is, the quality
and accuracy of those graph visualizations depend heavily on rigorous
data wrangling prior to analysis.
Bibliometric data exported from databases like WoSCC often contain
inconsistencies, duplicates, and unstructured metadata across key vari-
ables such as publication year, affiliation, and keywords [10]. Without
proper cleaning, restructuring, and filtering, the input data may lead to
misleading or cluttered visualizations. Therefore, data wrangling is a
foundational step to ensure that only statistically relevant and compa
rably formatted elements are fed into visualization tools like slope
graphs, ultimately enabling more precise and meaningful insights into
scholarly trends over time. Likewise, data wrangling before conducting
performance analysis of metadata entities is essential to ensure the
generation of reliable and interpretable summary reports. However, the
technique of ’data mugging’—the systematic extraction and restruc-
turing of key bibliometric fields—has received limited attention in
previous studies [1].
To close these gaps, there is a pressing need for a lightweight,
transparent, and reproducible Excel-based framework that facilitates
bibliometric analysis without depending on complex software environ-
ments. Such a solution would be especially valuable in educational
settings or for interdisciplinary researchers who may not have access to
specialized bibliometric platforms.
1.3. Challenges of reproducibility and transparency in bibliometric studies
Previous bibliometric case studies have struggled with reproduc
ibility and transparency due to incomplete disclosure of data-processing
steps and opaque workflows. As Liu [10] noted, reporting “Web of Sci-
ence Core Collection” without specifying subsets (e.g., SCI-Expanded,
SSCI), coverage years, or search date undermines reproducibility.
Moreover, database-focused studies document concrete inconsistencies
that can bias results, including coverage/indexing differences across
WoS and Scopus; incomplete or erroneous funding acknowledgments;
missing/ambiguous author–affiliation links; document-type and Early
Access mislabeling; uneven identifier coverage (ORCID/ResearcherID);
and variable availability of abstracts, Author Keywords, and Keywords
To address these issues, our framework operationalizes a trans-
parent, auditable pipeline: (i) record full data provenance (database,
subsets, years, search date); (ii) normalize authors, affiliations, docu
ment types, Early Access, and keyword fields; (iii) de-duplicate pri-
marily by DOI (with title-based fallback); (iv) log every transformation;
and (v) perform analyst-supervised identity checks that combine full
names with affiliation/country, using ORCID where available. The
workflow is implemented in Excel/VBA (“10StepsinExcelforWoS”) and
integrates DC analysis [11,12], thereby standardizing wrangling,
strengthening quality control, and improving reproducibility.
1.4. Study goal and contribution
This study proposes a novel framework titled 10StepsinExcelforWoS
(or ExcelWoS for short), which utilizes a 10-step VBA-powered process
in Microsoft Excel (MS Excel) to streamline bibliometric data wrangling,
visualization, and performance reporting. The method was applied to
analyze articles indexed in WoSCC. Two types of visual outputs were
generated:
(1) a summarized performance report [1] based on ten key met
adata elements, and
(2) Kano and Sankey diagrams [1,19–21] to identify dominant
countries in bibliometric publishing.
By validating this Excel-based approach, the study aims to enhance
the transparency, accessibility, and reproducibility of bibliometric
research. The framework also responds to growing demands for
simplified tools that support nuanced academic insights.
This study aims to evaluate whether a structured, VBA-powered
Excel workflow—implemented through the 10StepsinExcelforWoS
framework—can generate bibliometric visualizations and performance
analyses that are comparable in clarity and analytical value to those
produced by specialized software, while offering improved accessibility,
usability, and reproducibility.

10StepsinExcelforWoS Framework
raschonline.com/raschonline/wosextractdataabc2bkaa.zip
Fig. 1. 10StepsinExcelforWoS Framework through 10 steps for data mugging
with the MS Excel file in zip.
2.1.2. Five steps for extracting data from WoSCC
The following steps outline the procedure for extracting and orga
nizing data exported from WoSCC using the downloaded Excel tool [22]:
1. Insert Journal Impact Factors: Ensure that the Journal Impact
Factors (e.g., from Journal Citation Reports: Impact Factor List 2025
[24]) are deposited in Sheet1 of the spreadsheet.
2. Rename Downloaded Files Using R: Use the provided R script to
rename all Excel files downloaded into the wos folder. This ensures
consistent naming for batch processing [25].
3. Set File Path and Verify File List: Open the designated Excel file (e.
g., named data) and set the file path to:
C:\Users\user\Downloads\wos\
Confirm that the renamed file names are listed vertically from cell
A2 downward.
4. Activate VBA Import: Click the “From WoS in folder” macro button.
This will trigger the VBA automation process to import data from
each listed file.
5. Consolidate Data into ALL Worksheet: In the “ddd” worksheet,
click the icon labeled “Paste data into All in AG.” This action auto-
matically transfers and consolidates the imported data into the ALL
worksheet, ready for further data wrangling and analysis.
2.1.3. Keywords from keyplus to top 10 using R script
The R script [26] was applied to obtain top 10 keywords pasted to the
spreadsheet of author at the cell of A82 downward.
2.2. Software functionalities and steps for implementing excelwos
To emphasize the importance of reproducibility in bibliometric
research [27], we parsed the WoSCC Excel export fields (e.g., Authors,
Affiliations, Countries), in which multiple entries are separated by
semicolons (;). Using the split function in MS Excel VBA, we also marked
special tokens such as the corresponding author and their affiliation
details (e.g., Mengist, W (corresponding author)).
2.2.1. infographic design for 10StepsinExcelforWoS
Click on icons 1 to 10 in the two spreadsheets titled “ALL” and
“author,” following these 10 steps (Fig. 1):
2.2.2. Ten steps for arranging data in MS excel
1. Import data: Transfer content from cell AG1 to A1 in the ALL
spreadsheet.
2. Extract metadata categories: Use the Country field in the ALL
spreadsheet to extract metadata categories.
3. Calculate CJAL score: Compute the CJAL score using the pro-
vided metrics [28,29].
4. Extract metadata each: Collect all relevant metadata (e.g.,
keywords and KeyPlus) into the spreadsheet.
5. Obtain Top 10 elements: In the author spreadsheet, retrieve the
top 10 elements for each metadata entity.
6. Compute h-index by category: In column Y, calculate the h
index for each metadata category (excluding keywords).
7. Overall h-index: Refer to cell author!AD94 for the overall h-
index across all articles.
8. Calculate CJAL score for keywords: Use rows 82 to 91 in the
keyword section to calculate the CJAL score for each keyword
9. Keyword-specific h-index: Use columns V82 to Y82 to compute
the h-index [30] for each keyword.
10. Read summary report: Click on the spreadsheet titled
“10descriptionmap” to view the final summary report.
2.3. Sample code snippets
2.3,1. R platform for visuals using Kano and Sankey diagrams
It is recommended to use visual coding scripts [31] for generating
Kano and Sankey diagrams, utilizing a CSV file (e.g., country.csv) con-
taining keyword co-occurrence data. The resulting Kano diagram cate-
gorizes entities into four quadrants: Leader, Lone Wolf, Follower, and
Coworker. Classification is based on the Dominance Coefficient (DC)
[11,12], which quantifies relative influence. Leadership strength is
further divided into five tiers: Super
( \mathrm { D C } \ge 0 . 8 )
, Quasi-Super
( \mathrm { D C } \geq 0 . 7 ) ,
Strong
( \mathrm { D C } \geq 0 . 6 )
, Moderate
( \mathrm { D C } \geq 0 . 5 ) _ { \mathrm { : } }
, and Weak
( \mathrm { D C } < 0 . 5 )
such, incorporating DC with KD [19,21] (or Sankey diagram[1]) en-
hances clarity by illustrating dominance or imbalance across metadata
entities, offering more insightful bibliometric evaluation.
Based on structured reports suggested by authors [1], the findings
were presented in two subsections: (1) Performance Analysis Findings
and (2) Visualization Outputs.
2.3.2 R package used in this study
Visualizations in R created on the R platform [31] were used to draw
Kano and Sankey diagrams. All data processing and statistical analyses
were conducted using R software version 4.1.3 [33], and the generation
of time-series visualizations and result output was performed within the
RStudio integrated development environment [34].

details of the dataset used in this study. Articles were retrieved from the
Web of Science Core Collection (WoSCC), including both the Science
Citation Index Expanded (SCI-Expanded) and the Social Sciences Cita-
tion Index (SSCI). The coverage period was from 2017 to 2025, with the
search conducted on July 29, 2025. By specifying both the subsets and
the temporal coverage, this study ensures full transparency and facili-
tates reproducibility for future bibliometric investigations.
These articles were retrieved to identify leading metadata categories
and verify the study hypothesis. Study data are deposed in Github [35].

In line with recommendations by Liu [10], we explicitly disclose the
details of the dataset used in this study. Articles were retrieved from the
Web of Science Core Collection (WoSCC), including both the Science
Citation Index Expanded (SCI-Expanded) and the Social Sciences Cita-
tion Index (SSCI). The coverage period was from 2017 to 2025, with the
search conducted on July 29, 2025. By specifying both the subsets and
the temporal coverage, this study ensures full transparency and facili-
tates reproducibility for future bibliometric investigations.
These articles were retrieved to identify leading metadata categories
and verify the study hypothesis. Study data are deposed in Github [35].

3.2. Demonstrations of data via 10StepsinExcelforWoS
3.2.1 Performance analysis findings
Fig. 2 displays a performance summary report outlining major con-
tributors and corresponding counts across ten key metadata categories
in bibliometric research from 2017 to 2025. The analysis incorporates
metrics such as the number of publications by corresponding authors
(RP), first authors (FP), h-index values [30], and DC scores [11,12]. In
total, 1719 articles were analyzed, with an overall h-index of 48.
Key insights drawn from the performance report include the leading
contribution of United States, with Delft Univ Technol (Netherlands) as
the most prolific institution, and the Department of Computer Science as
the most frequently listed organizational affiliation. Wojciech Salabun
from Poland emerged as the most productive author, and SoftwareX as
the most common journal as expected. Other dominant attributes
include the year 2024, the document type "Article", the Department of
Computer Science as the most prevalent affiliation—appearing across 60
universities for first authors and 42 for corresponding authors, and the
most frequent keyword “MODEL” Notably, the most cited pub
lication—a 2018 article by Susi Lehtola(U.S)—received 551 citations.
Among all top-performing entities, only the document type "Article"
achieved a DC score above 0.70 (DC = 0.99), suggesting that no other
entity held a clearly dominant position (i.e., >0.7) within its respective
category during the study period.
3.2.2 Visualization outputs
Author collaborations and co-keyword occurrences were clustered
using Follower-Leading Clustering algorithm(FLCA) [1,21,36]. Top 20
elements were selected and shown on either Kano or Sankey diagram.
United States (Fig. 3) emerges as a strong leader with a DC of 0.60.
In contrast, Politecn Torino(Italy) is not classified as a leader (Fig. 4)
due to limited collaborative influence in the field, while the keyword
“MODEL” (Fig. 5) represents a strong leader (DC = 0.61).
3.4. To tests the study hypothesis
The findings of this study confirm that a structured, VBA-driven
Excel workflow—implemented through the ExcelWoS framework—can
successfully generate bibliometric visualizations and performance ana-
lyses that are comparable in clarity and analytical value to those (e.g.,
shown in Table 1) produced by any specialized bibliometric software,
while providing enhanced accessibility, usability, and reproducibility
for researchers, as shown in author-made MS-Excel module [22] and
instruction with MP4 video [23].
4. Impact
The ExcelWoS tool introduces a new capability in bibliometric
research by automating data wrangling for downstream analysis—a
function not available in any of the 10,248 PubMed-indexed biblio-
metric studies to date [36]. This transition from manual data handling to
automated resolution with ExcelWoS unlocks several novel research
avenues. For example, researchers can now analyze disciplinary char-
acteristics by article category with clear and concise bibliometric out-
puts [1], and make comparisons across institutions or countries—task
that previously required cumbersome tables and graphs.
ExcelWoS significantly advances the pursuit of existing bibliometric
questions by enhancing both the granularity and automation of the data-
wrangling process. In contrast to traditional tools such as VOSviewer
[3], Bibliometrix [4], and CiteSpace [2], which lack built-in data
preparation capabilities, ExcelWoS integrates FLCA-based clustering [1,
37] alongside Kano and Sankey diagram visualizations [1,19,20,32].
This integration streamlines bibliometric workflows and minimizes the
need for manual curation.
In practice, ExcelWoS has already facilitated the extraction of
extensive metadata for downstream analyses. The accompanying R
scripts [9] are designed for user-friendliness, allowing researchers
without advanced programming expertise to conduct bibliometric ana-
lyses efficiently. Early adopters [1,6–8] have reported significant re-
ductions in metadata preparation time and enhanced clarity in
translating metadata into a structured format. ExcelWoS for future

5. Conclusion
This study introduces ExcelWoS, a lightweight yet powerful VBA-
driven framework that addresses critical gaps in bibliometric work
flows, particularly for researchers relying on Excel-exported data from
WoSCC. By automating ten essential steps—including data wrangling,
performance reporting, and visualization—ExcelWoS enhances the
reproducibility, accessibility, and interpretability of bibliometric ana-
lyses. It integrates advanced features such as FLCA clustering and
dominance coefficient (DC) scoring, producing insightful visual outputs
like summary reports, Kano diagrams, and Sankey diagrams.
As a transparent and reproducible framework, ExcelWoS offers
strong potential for integration into institutional dashboards, library
systems, and future SaaS platforms. Ultimately, ExcelWoS democratizes
bibliometric analysis, streamlines scholarly evaluation, and opens new
avenues for trend discovery and academic decision-making.
